definition: Reduction in received radio power as the transmitter and receiver move farther apart.
wrongs: A coding overhead added so the receiver can detect bit errors.
The time an idle phone waits before it answers a page.
A sudden hardware fault that mutes only the base-station clock.
why: Radiated energy spreads and is absorbed, so less power arrives as range increases.
example: A handset two kilometres from a tower receives far less power than one at 200 metres.
scenario: Doubling the range from a tower drops received power by several decibels even on a clear path. Which effect explains that drop?
scenarioWhy: Received power falls with distance because the wave spreads, which is path loss.

definition: Line-of-sight power loss caused only by geometric spreading, with no obstacles or ground reflections.
wrongs: Loss caused by hills blocking an otherwise short radio hop.
Loss inserted by a channel code before modulation.
Loss that appears only when two cells reuse one channel.
why: In free space the same energy is spread over a larger sphere as range grows.
example: A clear satellite downlink loses power with both distance and carrier frequency.
scenario: A rooftop microwave budget, with a clear line of sight, includes a loss that grows with frequency and distance. Which loss is that?
scenarioWhy: With no obstacles, distance and frequency loss is free-space path loss.

definition: Travel of one transmitted signal along several reflected, diffracted, or scattered paths.
wrongs: Transmission of independent users on separate assigned frequencies.
A single optical fibre path from a studio to a tower.
Encryption of one packet into several cipher blocks.
why: Buildings and the ground create copies that arrive at different times.
example: On a city street the same beacon reaches a phone from a wall, a bus, and the road.
scenario: A receiver recording shows three delayed copies of one transmitted pulse. Which propagation effect produced those copies?
scenarioWhy: Distinct delayed copies mean the signal took more than one path.

definition: Variation of received signal strength over time or position caused by multipath or obstruction.
wrongs: A fixed amplifier gain chosen once when the site is built.
The steady loss of a cable of unchanging length.
A scheduled reduction of transmit power at night.
why: Multipath copies add and cancel, and obstacles change, so amplitude is not steady.
example: Walking a few metres indoors makes phone signal bars rise and fall although the tower is unchanged.
scenario: A seated laptop holds a steady Wi-Fi rate, but pacing the same room makes the rate swing. Which channel effect is the walking user seeing?
scenarioWhy: Small movements change how multipath copies combine, which is fading.

definition: Small-scale fading when many scattered paths arrive and no line-of-sight path dominates.
wrongs: Fading dominated by one strong direct path plus weak echoes.
A purely deterministic loss that never varies with position.
Slow blockage by a single large building only.
why: With no dominant path the quadrature components are roughly Gaussian, so the envelope is Rayleigh.
example: A downtown pedestrian whose tower is hidden by blocks of flats sees a Rayleigh envelope.
scenario: A campus model assumes no line of sight and many similar scatterers around the handset. Which envelope distribution fits?
scenarioWhy: Many scattered paths and no dominant path give a Rayleigh envelope.

definition: Small-scale fading when a strong line-of-sight path arrives together with weaker scattered paths.
wrongs: Fading with no dominant path at all.
Only the slow shadow of a hill, with no multipath.
Interference from a neighbouring frequency plan.
why: The steady direct component changes the envelope from Rayleigh to Rician.
example: A drone that can see a rooftop radio, while still catching wall echoes, experiences Rician fading.
scenario: A rural link has one strong direct path plus a few ground reflections. Which fading model fits that mix?
scenarioWhy: A dominant path plus weaker scatterers is the Rician case.

definition: Slow change in local-mean received power caused by large obstacles blocking the path.
wrongs: Fast ripple of amplitude over a few wavelengths from multipath.
A Doppler shift of the carrier frequency.
Intentional power reduction commanded by the scheduler.
why: Hills and buildings attenuate the whole signal for many metres, unlike fast multipath ripple.
example: Driving behind a hill drops a call's average level by about 10 dB until the ridge clears.
scenario: Over hundreds of metres the local mean wobbles as vans and buildings block a street-level user. Which large-scale effect is that?
scenarioWhy: Obstacle blockage of the local mean is shadowing, often modelled as log-normal.

definition: Change in observed carrier frequency when transmitter and receiver move relative to each other.
wrongs: A time offset caused only by a longer propagation path.
A phase code applied by the modulator on purpose.
A frequency error from an unlicensed Wi-Fi channel plan.
why: Motion changes how fast wave crests arrive, so the received frequency moves.
example: A handset in a car approaching a tower hears a slightly higher carrier than the one transmitted.
scenario: A high-speed train receiver sees the downlink carrier move by several hundred hertz. Which motion effect is that?
scenarioWhy: Relative speed changes the received frequency, which is Doppler shift.

definition: The time interval over which the channel impulse response stays approximately constant.
wrongs: The gap between the first and last multipath echoes.
The frequency band over which fading stays correlated.
The slot length assigned to one GSM user.
why: Motion changes multipath phases at a rate set by Doppler spread, which fixes this interval.
example: A pedestrian channel stays similar for milliseconds, while a bullet-train channel changes sooner.
scenario: A designer needs how long one channel estimate remains usable for a moving user. Which quantity is that interval?
scenarioWhy: The time the channel stays steady is the coherence time.

definition: The range of frequencies over which the channel gain remains highly correlated.
wrongs: The time for which a channel estimate stays valid.
The total licensed spectrum of an operator.
The Doppler shift of the fastest user.
why: Large delay spread makes frequencies fade differently, so this range becomes narrower.
example: A channel with tiny delay spread stays correlated across a whole 200 kHz GSM carrier.
scenario: Engineers compare the signal bandwidth with the band where the gain stays similar. Which channel measure is that band?
scenarioWhy: Correlation of fading across frequency is the coherence bandwidth.

definition: The time span between the earliest and latest significant copies of a multipath signal.
wrongs: How long the channel gain stays constant in time.
The duration of one OFDM cyclic prefix by definition only.
The round-trip time of a core-network ping.
why: Different path lengths make copies of the same symbol arrive spread out in time.
example: In a hilly suburb the last strong echo of a pulse arrives 3 microseconds after the first.
scenario: Sounding shows the first echo at 0.2 microseconds and the last strong echo at 4 microseconds. Which quantity is about 3.8 microseconds?
scenarioWhy: The span from the first to the last significant echo is the delay spread.

definition: Fading in which every frequency in the signal bandwidth sees nearly the same gain.
wrongs: Fading that puts a deep notch in only part of the signal band.
A fade that always changes inside one symbol.
Interference that arrives only from the adjacent carrier.
why: This occurs when the signal bandwidth is much smaller than the coherence bandwidth.
example: A narrowband paging tone fades up and down as a whole, with no notch inside its spectrum.
scenario: A 25 kHz signal has a coherence bandwidth of several hundred kilohertz. Which fading type should the link assume?
scenarioWhy: A signal narrower than the coherence bandwidth sees flat fading.

definition: Fading in which different frequencies inside the signal bandwidth experience different gains.
wrongs: Fading that scales the whole signal spectrum by one gain.
Slow shadowing that is identical at every frequency.
A filter that removes an entire licensed band on purpose.
why: A large delay spread makes the frequency response vary and can cause inter-symbol interference.
example: An urban LTE resource block shows a deep notch on some subcarriers but not on others.
scenario: A wideband waveform sees a notch that removes only part of its spectrum. Which fading type is that?
scenarioWhy: A notch across only part of the band is frequency-selective fading.

definition: Fading that changes appreciably within one symbol, so the gain is not constant over that symbol.
wrongs: Fading that stays fixed for many symbols.
A shadow that changes only when the user turns a corner.
Fading that is identical on every subcarrier.
why: The coherence time is then shorter than the symbol duration.
example: A very long satellite symbol changes gain before it ends because the terminal is moving quickly.
scenario: The coherence time is shorter than the symbol period, so one symbol sees a changing gain. Which fading speed is that?
scenarioWhy: A channel that varies inside a symbol is fast fading.

definition: Fading that stays nearly constant over many successive symbols.
wrongs: Fading that changes inside every symbol.
A different gain on every subcarrier at one instant.
An instantaneous Doppler jump once per bit.
why: The coherence time is then much longer than the symbol duration, so one estimate covers a burst.
example: At walking speed an LTE channel estimate is reused across a subframe because the fade is slow.
scenario: Estimates taken once per subframe stay valid for dozens of symbols at pedestrian speed. Which fading speed is that?
scenarioWhy: A gain that holds over many symbols is slow fading.

definition: The geographic service area covered by one base-station site and its radio channels.
wrongs: The entire country served by one mobile operator.
A location area made of many sites used only for paging.
The core-network database that stores subscriber profiles.
why: Users in that area are served by that site, which is the basic unit of a cellular plan.
example: A suburban tower planned for about a 2 kilometre radius forms one cell on the operator map.
scenario: Planners draw a hexagon around one tower to show the area that tower is meant to serve. Which planning unit is the hexagon?
scenarioWhy: The area served by one base-station site is a cell.

definition: Assigning the same carrier frequencies again in cells that are far enough apart.
wrongs: Giving every cell in the network a completely unique band.
Hopping a single call across all channels each burst.
Encrypting the same bits with a repeated cipher key.
why: Distance lowers co-channel interference, so a limited band can serve many cells.
example: Channel 45 is used in a north-side cell and again in a cell four sites away.
scenario: An operator has only 60 voice channels but hundreds of cells. Which planning method lets distant cells share those channels?
scenarioWrongs: A unique band for every cell
scenarioWhy: Sharing carriers among distant cells is frequency reuse.

definition: The number of cells that together use each channel once before the reuse pattern repeats.
wrongs: The number of sectors on a single tower.
The number of time slots inside one GSM frame.
The radius of a cell measured in kilometres.
why: A larger cluster separates co-channel cells more, trading capacity per cell for less interference.
example: A seven-cell cluster means each channel appears once in every group of seven cells.
scenario: Hexagonal planning uses shift parameters i=2 and j=1. How many cells are in one cluster?
scenarioWhy: Cluster size is i squared plus i times j plus j squared, which equals 7.

definition: Interference from other transmitters that operate on the same carrier frequency.
wrongs: Leakage from a transmitter on the next carrier frequency.
Noise generated inside the receiver's own electronics.
A delayed copy of the wanted signal from the same transmitter.
why: Reuse places the same channel in other cells, and those signals enter the victim receiver.
example: A call on channel 12 is degraded by another cell transmitting on channel 12 three sites away.
scenario: Two distant cells both use 935.2 MHz, and each phone hears the other cell. Which interference is that?
scenarioWhy: The same carrier used in another cell produces co-channel interference.

definition: Interference from energy that leaks into the receiver from a neighbouring carrier.
wrongs: Interference from a distant cell on the identical carrier.
A fade caused only by two multipath copies cancelling.
Noise that does not depend on any other transmitter.
why: Imperfect filters and transmitter masks let nearby frequencies spill into the wanted channel.
example: A strong signal 200 kHz above a GSM carrier raises the floor in the wanted receiver.
scenario: A handset tuned to carrier f is disturbed by a nearby tower on the next 200 kHz carrier. Which interference is that?
scenarioWhy: Leakage from the next carrier is adjacent-channel interference.

definition: Transfer of an ongoing mobile connection from one base station to another.
wrongs: An idle phone's report that it entered a new location area.
A broadcast asking an idle phone to answer a call.
The first registration after the phone is switched on.
why: As the user moves, the radio link must follow the cell with the better signal.
example: A voice call stays up while a car crosses from a city cell into a motorway cell.
scenario: During a live call the serving signal falls and a neighbour becomes stronger, so the network moves the radio link. Which procedure is that?
scenarioWhy: Moving an active connection between cells is a handover.

definition: A cell change that releases the old radio link before the new link is established.
wrongs: A cell change that keeps two base-station links up together.
An idle reselections with no active call.
A core-network restart that drops every session.
why: The mobile cannot hold both channels at once, so there is a short break-before-make gap.
example: A GSM phone leaves its old traffic channel and only then uses the new cell's channel.
scenario: A GSM call drops the old traffic channel and only afterwards uses the new cell. Which handover style is that?
scenarioWhy: Releasing the old link before the new one is hard handover.

definition: A cell change during which the mobile keeps radio links to more than one base station.
wrongs: A break-before-make change that uses only one link at a time.
A change of IP address with no radio involvement.
A forced release of the call when load is high.
why: CDMA can combine the same signal from several sites before one link is dropped.
example: A UMTS phone at a cell edge exchanges traffic with two Node Bs at the same time.
scenario: A CDMA phone stays in the active set of two base stations and combines both downlinks. Which handover style is that?
scenarioWhy: Holding links to two base stations at once is soft handover.

definition: An extra signal margin a neighbour must exceed before a handover is allowed.
wrongs: The minimum power a phone may use on any channel.
The number of cells in a reuse cluster.
The delay added by a speech transcoder.
why: The margin stops switching when two cell signals are nearly equal and fluctuating.
example: A neighbour must be at least 3 dB stronger than the serving cell before the call moves.
scenario: Two cells differ by only 1 dB and the required margin is 3 dB, so the call stays. Which parameter is blocking the move?
scenarioWhy: The extra margin that must be cleared is handover hysteresis.

definition: Rapid repeated handovers of the same connection back and forth between two cells.
wrongs: A single successful move from a weak cell to a strong cell.
Combining two downlinks without releasing either.
An idle phone updating its location once per day.
why: Signal fluctuation around a tight threshold reverses the handover decision again and again.
example: A phone standing on a boundary is moved between two towers four times in one minute.
scenario: A stationary user on a boundary is switched between two cells every few seconds. Which handover fault is that?
scenarioWhy: Oscillating between two cells is ping-pong handover.

definition: A message from an idle mobile reporting that it has entered a new location area.
wrongs: A move of an active traffic channel to a new cell.
A network broadcast searching for one idle phone.
A measurement of neighbour cells during a call.
why: The network stores that area so it later knows where to page the mobile.
example: After a bus crosses a location-area border, the idle phone updates the network and returns to idle.
scenario: An idle phone enters a new location area and must tell the network before the next incoming call. Which message does it send?
scenarioWhy: Idle mobiles report a new location area with a location update.

definition: A network broadcast that asks one specific idle mobile to respond to an incoming session.
wrongs: An idle mobile telling the network its new location area.
Transfer of an active call to a stronger cell.
A request for an uplink grant to send a photo.
why: The network often knows only the location area, so it calls the mobile across that area.
example: When a friend dials the number, cells in the stored area broadcast that phone's paging identity.
scenario: An idle subscriber is called, and base stations in the stored area broadcast a request for that handset. Which procedure is the broadcast?
scenarioWhy: Searching an area for an idle mobile is paging.

definition: A second-generation cellular standard that uses TDMA and GMSK on 200 kHz carriers.
wrongs: A fourth-generation system with OFDMA and an all-IP core.
A short-range personal radio that hops in the 2.4 GHz band.
An analogue first-generation system with one FM channel per user.
why: GSM carries digital voice in eight time slots on each 200 kHz GMSK carrier.
example: A classic GSM voice call occupies one of eight slots on a 200 kHz carrier near 900 MHz.
scenario: A legacy network puts eight users in successive slots on one 200 kHz GMSK carrier. Which cellular standard is that?
scenarioWhy: Eight-slot TDMA and GMSK on 200 kHz carriers identify GSM.

definition: Sharing one carrier by giving each user a distinct repeating time slot.
wrongs: Giving each user a separate frequency at the same time.
Separating users only by spreading codes.
Letting every user transmit whenever the channel looks idle.
why: Users transmit in turn, so they are separated in time on the same frequency.
example: On a GSM carrier, one user transmits only in slot 3 of every frame.
scenario: Four users share one frequency, each sending only in its own repeating slot. Which multiple-access method is that?
scenarioWhy: Separation by time slots on one carrier is TDMA.

definition: Sharing a band by assigning each user a distinct frequency channel.
wrongs: Assigning users different time slots on one shared carrier.
Assigning users different spreading codes on one carrier.
Assigning groups of orthogonal subcarriers that can change each slot.
why: Filters and guard bands keep users apart because they occupy different frequencies together.
example: An older trunked radio gives each active call its own 12.5 kHz channel at the same time.
scenario: Three calls run at once on 825, 825.03, and 825.06 MHz with no time sharing. Which access method is that?
scenarioWhy: Distinct frequencies used at the same time are FDMA.

definition: Sharing time and frequency while separating users with unique spreading codes.
wrongs: Separating users only by carrier frequency.
Separating users only by time slot.
Serving only one user in the whole cell at a time.
why: A receiver despreads its own code and treats other users as interference.
example: Two UMTS phones transmit together in the same 5 MHz block and are separated by codes.
scenario: Several users occupy the same 5 MHz block at the same time and are separated only by codes. Which access method is that?
scenarioWhy: Code separation on a shared carrier is CDMA.

definition: Sharing a band by assigning different groups of orthogonal subcarriers to different users.
wrongs: Giving each user one wide non-overlapping analogue channel.
Separating users only with spreading codes.
Letting stations contend with random backoff.
why: Orthogonal subcarriers can be packed tightly and grouped to follow each user's channel.
example: An LTE downlink gives one phone 12 subcarriers and another phone a different group in the same symbol.
scenario: A scheduler gives user A subcarriers 0-11 and user B subcarriers 24-35 in the same symbol. Which access method is that?
scenarioWhy: Assigning groups of orthogonal subcarriers is OFDMA.

definition: A fourth-generation cellular system using OFDMA downlink, SC-FDMA uplink, and an all-IP core.
wrongs: A 2G system of eight GMSK time slots on 200 kHz.
A 3G wideband CDMA system with a circuit-switched core.
A personal-area hop radio for headsets.
why: LTE schedules packet data on a shared OFDMA carrier and does not use circuit-switched radio bearers.
example: A smartphone download is scheduled as resource blocks on a 20 MHz LTE carrier.
scenario: A 4G air interface uses OFDMA toward the phone, SC-FDMA from the phone, and an all-IP core. Which system is that?
scenarioWhy: OFDMA downlink, SC-FDMA uplink, and an all-IP core identify LTE.

definition: The fifth-generation New Radio interface, with scalable subcarrier spacing and massive MIMO support.
wrongs: A 2G standard locked to 200 kHz GMSK carriers.
A wireless LAN standard in the IEEE 802.11 family.
A 4G system whose subcarrier spacing is fixed at 15 kHz.
why: NR numerology lets one design serve wide millimetre-wave carriers and short low-latency slots.
example: A stadium radio uses 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and a large array near 28 GHz.
scenario: A new air interface can select 15, 30, or 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and large antenna arrays. Which standard is that?
scenarioWhy: Scalable subcarrier spacing is a defining feature of 5G NR.

definition: A low-power base station that covers a short range, such as a street, room, or venue.
wrongs: A high tower planned to cover several kilometres.
A core router that switches packets between cities.
A handset operating as a measuring tool only.
why: Short range lets spectrum be reused densely and fills gaps a macro site covers poorly.
example: A cafe installs a low-power cellular radio that covers the shop and the pavement outside.
scenario: An operator adds a low-power node for one railway platform and keeps the macro tower. Which site type is the new node?
scenarioWhy: A low-power, short-range base station is a small cell.

definition: Use of multiple antennas at both ends to send several spatial data streams on one frequency.
wrongs: Repeating one stream on separated antennas only to survive a fade.
Assigning each antenna a different licensed band.
Hopping one stream across many carriers.
why: Scattering makes the spatial paths different enough for the receiver to separate the streams.
example: A Wi-Fi access point with three antennas sends two spatial streams to a two-antenna laptop.
scenario: A link uses four transmit and four receive antennas to carry four independent streams on one carrier. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Multiple independent spatial streams are MIMO.

definition: Weighting an antenna array so more radiated energy is aimed toward a chosen user.
wrongs: Radiating equally in every direction from one dipole.
Splitting users by orthogonal codes.
Compressing the user data before transmission.
why: Phase weights make the waves add toward the user and partly cancel elsewhere.
example: A 5G panel steers a narrow beam that follows one phone as it moves across a hall.
scenario: An array applies phase shifts so the downlink adds up at one handset and is weaker elsewhere. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Steering array energy toward one user is beamforming.

definition: A base-station array with very many antennas serving many users on the same time-frequency resources.
wrongs: A single rooftop dipole covering a sector.
Two antennas used only to pick the stronger branch.
A Wi-Fi contention network with one antenna.
why: Dozens or hundreds of antennas form tight beams and separate users in space.
example: A campus tower with 64 antennas serves eight phones on the same resource blocks.
scenario: A site uses 64 antennas to beamform many phones at once on the same subcarriers. Which architecture is that?
scenarioWhy: A very large array serving many co-channel users is massive MIMO.

definition: The IEEE 802.11 family of wireless local-area networks, usually operated in unlicensed bands.
wrongs: A licensed cellular standard with a SIM and a core network.
A one-hop satellite broadcast toward fixed dishes.
A wired Ethernet standard over twisted pair.
why: 802.11 defines wireless LAN frames, contention access, and bands such as 2.4 and 5 GHz.
example: A lecture-hall laptop joins an 802.11 network advertised by the campus SSID.
scenario: Students connect laptops to an IEEE 802.11 access point in the unlicensed 5 GHz band. Which technology is that?
scenarioWhy: An IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN is Wi-Fi.

definition: A Wi-Fi access method that listens for a busy medium and waits a random backoff before sending.
wrongs: Detecting collisions on a coaxial cable while transmitting.
A base station assigning every user a fixed slot.
Sending immediately with no sensing and no backoff.
why: A wireless sender cannot reliably hear a collision while it transmits, so it tries to avoid one.
example: Two laptops both find the medium idle, then each waits a different random backoff.
scenario: A station senses the medium and, if it is idle, still waits a random number of slots before a data frame. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Listen-before-talk with random backoff is CSMA/CA.

definition: A station that cannot hear another sender even though both can collide at the same receiver.
wrongs: A station that defers because it hears a sender, though its own destination is clear.
Two phones separated by codes on a CDMA carrier.
A node whose signal captures the receiver despite a weaker collision.
why: Distance or an obstacle hides one sender, so carrier sense does not prevent a collision.
example: Laptops on opposite sides of a pillar both transmit to one access point and corrupt each other.
scenario: Station A cannot hear station B, yet their frames collide at the access point between them. Which problem is that?
scenarioWhy: Mutually hidden senders colliding at the receiver are a hidden node.

definition: A short-range personal-area radio that frequency-hops in the 2.4 GHz band.
wrongs: A cellular wide-area standard managed by a mobile operator.
A wireless LAN access-point standard for whole buildings.
A long-haul microwave link between hilltop towers.
why: Classic Bluetooth hops among 79 one-megahertz channels to live with other 2.4 GHz users.
example: A headset stays linked to a phone across a room on a shared Bluetooth hop sequence.
scenario: A headset and a phone keep a short-range 2.4 GHz link that hops across dozens of channels. Which technology fits?
scenarioWhy: A short-range frequency-hopping personal link is Bluetooth.

definition: Changing the carrier many times per second using a sequence known to both ends.
wrongs: Spreading each bit by a fast code while staying on one carrier.
Keeping one fixed channel for the whole session.
Assigning a permanent frequency in a cellular cluster plan.
why: A narrow interferer then damages only some hops, and the link can recover the others.
example: A radio dwells on 2402 MHz, then 2430 MHz, then 2475 MHz, following a shared pattern.
scenario: A link changes carrier 1600 times per second using a sequence the receiver already knows. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: A shared rapid sequence of carriers is frequency hopping.

definition: A modulation that maps each two-bit group to one of four carrier phases 90 degrees apart.
wrongs: A modulation with only two phases, carrying one bit per symbol.
A square grid that uses several amplitudes as well as phases.
On-off keying that turns the carrier on or off.
why: Four phases carry two bits per symbol and can keep a constant envelope.
example: Successive symbols use the phases 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees for bit pairs.
scenario: A constellation has four points on a circle, each representing a different two-bit pair. Which modulation is that?
scenarioWhy: Four equally spaced phases and two bits per symbol identify QPSK.

definition: A modulation that encodes bits in both the amplitude and the phase of the carrier.
wrongs: A two-phase modulation that carries only one bit per symbol.
Frequency-shift keying between two tones.
Pulse-position modulation with a constant carrier amplitude.
why: A rectangular constellation packs several bits into one symbol when the link is strong enough.
example: A strong Wi-Fi link uses 64-QAM so that each symbol carries six bits.
scenario: A constellation is a square grid of several amplitudes and phases, with six bits on each symbol. Which family is that?
scenarioWhy: A grid that uses both amplitude and phase is QAM.

definition: Changing modulation and coding during a session to match the current channel quality.
wrongs: Keeping one constellation and code rate for the whole session.
Planning reuse distances on a paper frequency map.
Authenticating the SIM before any data flows.
why: A strong channel can use a denser constellation, while a weak channel needs a tougher mode.
example: As a user walks toward the tower, the scheduler moves the LTE MCS from QPSK toward 64-QAM.
scenario: The scheduler selects a higher-order constellation only after the reported channel quality improves. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Matching modulation and code rate to channel quality is link adaptation.

definition: Carrying the same information on separated antennas so one fade is unlikely to hit every copy.
wrongs: Sending independent data streams on the same antennas.
Compressing the source to fewer bits.
Splitting a site into directional sectors with different channels.
why: Antennas spaced by a fraction of a wavelength see partly independent multipath.
example: A base station selects the stronger of two rooftop antennas when one sits in a deep fade.
scenario: Two receive antennas carry the same stream, and the receiver keeps the stronger branch. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Separated antennas protecting one stream provide spatial diversity.

definition: Dividing one site into angular sectors, each served by a directional antenna.
wrongs: Covering the whole site with one omnidirectional antenna.
Combining two sites during a soft handover.
Hopping every sector through the same single channel.
why: Each sector sees a smaller angle of interference and can carry its own channels.
example: A tower uses three 120-degree panels, each with its own channel set.
scenario: One site is split into three 120-degree panels, and each panel has its own channels. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Directional panels that split a site are sectorisation.

definition: Network functions that track where a mobile is and keep its session as it moves between cells.
wrongs: Billing the subscriber at the end of the month.
Manufacturing the handset antenna.
Compressing speech before it enters the channel coder.
why: It includes idle-area tracking and active handover so reachability and sessions survive motion.
example: During a commute the core updates the tracking area and the radio network hands over the bearer.
scenario: Packets must still arrive after a user changes cells and later enters a new tracking area. Which function set handles that?
scenarioWhy: Tracking location and maintaining sessions during motion is mobility management.

definition: The ratio of wanted signal power to the sum of interference power and noise power.
wrongs: Received signal strength with no comparison to interference or noise.
The delay between the first and last multipath echoes.
The number of cells that share one reuse pattern.
why: Both interference and noise corrupt symbols, so schedulers and decoders use this ratio.
example: A cell-edge phone whose signal is 10 dB above interference plus noise has a SINR of 10 dB.
scenario: A scheduler compares wanted power with interference plus noise before choosing a modulation. Which metric is it using?
scenarioWhy: Wanted power over interference plus noise is SINR.
